newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Cholera epidemic in Zaire refugee camp hits airlift.
newsitem.headline: Cholera epidemic in Zaire refugee camp hits airlift.

text.p: A cholera epidemic was declared among Rwandan Hutu refugees in rebel-held eastern Zaire on Sunday, threatening a long delay for a planned repatriation airlift.
The senior local official of the World Health Organisation (WHO) announced the epidemic after five cholera deaths on April 7 and 8 in the Kasese 2 refugee site, 29 km (17 miles) south of Kisangani.
About 50,000 Rwandan refugees are camped out at Kasese with a similar number in makeshift camps further south.
The announcement was certain to delay plans to repatriate the 100,000 refugees, WHO official Leonard Kinuani told Reuters by telephone from Kisangani .

"Up to April 9 in the Kasese 2 site we had recorded 120 cases requiring hospital treament of whom five died," said Kinuani, a Zairean. "This formal declaration of an epidemic will delay the repatriation until it is brought under control."
The first flights had been expected in the next few days but Kinuani said it might take a month to declare the refugees cholera-free.
"We have to fear that there is the same cholera problem in the other sites," Kinuani said, adding that tests continued. The 10,000-strong local Zairean population was also at risk.

WHO and both Zairean and foreign doctors will isolate the sick and try to arrange 24-hour medical care in the camps, Kinuani said. Aid workers began last week trying to purify the water supply from a nearby river.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said on Sunday 93 deaths among the refugees south of Kisangani were reported on Friday, a high toll but down from 180 the previous Friday.
The refugees are the rump of more than two million Rwandan Hutus who fled their country in July 1994 after the victory of Tutsi rebels in the civil war.
Most returned home late last year but about 300,000 are believed to be stranded in Zaire, with the largest concentration between Kisangani and Ubundi, 125 km (75 miles) to the south.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR is planning a hugely expensive airlift to repatriate the Hutus, who now say they want to go home.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila was put under international pressure this month to agree to the airlift after earlier insisting the refugees should be trucked home, though the roads are impassable for long stretches.

In what diplomats said was a gesture to help get Kabila's agreement for the airlift, international relief agencies are flying internally displaced Zaireans back to their home towns in eastern Zaire from Kisangani.
Kinuani said the type of cholera found among patients at Kasese 2 was Inaba.

The refugees are in an appalling state after trekking about 600 km (375 miles) since last October through dense jungle where they survived on grubs and tree-bark. They marched westwards further into Zaire to flee Kabila's rebellion which is supported by the Rwandan government.

But Kabila now controls half of Zaire and the capture of Kisangani on March 15 led most refugees to end their flight and agree to go home. Many fear arrest for their suspected role in the genocide of Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda in 1994.
